title: Classes and Instances
relevance: Interviewers check that candidates can model stateful objects with a class blueprint, instantiate them, and attach per-object state via __init__ and self.

phases.goal: Establish a class as a blueprint and an instance as a concrete object created from it.

must_hit.point: A class is a user-defined blueprint or prototype from which objects are created.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate calls a class a blueprint/prototype used to create objects, not the object itself.

must_hit.point: An instance (object) is a specific realization created from that class blueprint.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts one class with multiple distinct instances that each realize the blueprint.

must_hit.point: A class is defined with the class keyword; an empty body can use pass and is still a valid class.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes or describes class Dog: pass and treats it as a usable class.

must_hit.point: Instantiation creates an object by calling the class as if it were a function (e.g. Dog()).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says you call the class like a function to get an instance, and may note type(my_dog) shows the Dog class.

probes: What is the difference between a class and an instance, and how do you create an instance from a class in Python?

hints.1: Think blueprint versus the concrete thing built from that blueprint.
hints.2: Mention the class keyword to define, then calling the class name with parentheses to instantiate.
hints.3: A class is the blueprint; my_dog = Dog() instantiates it, and type(my_dog) reports the Dog class.

phases.goal: Explain how attributes, methods, __init__, and self give each object lasting state and behavior.

must_hit.point: A class bundles state as attributes (data on the object) and behavior as methods (functions defined inside the class body).
__init__ is a special method automatically invoked whenever a new instance is created, used to initialize instance attributes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says __init__ runs on construction and sets things like self.name and self.age.

must_hit.point: self refers to the specific instance being operated on; without self, names in __init__ are temporary locals that disappear when the method finishes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains self attaches values to that object's memory; bare locals would not persist on the instance.

must_hit.point: If an instance method omits self as its first parameter, calling it on an instance raises TypeError because Python automatically passes the instance as the first argument.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names TypeError and that Python injects the instance as the invisible first argument.

must_hit.point: Calling an instance method on the class and passing the instance explicitly (e.g. Dog.bark(buddy)) works the same as calling it on the instance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says Dog.bark(buddy) is equivalent to buddy.bark() because the instance is passed as the first argument.

probes: What do __init__ and self do when you create an object, and what goes wrong if you leave self out of an instance method?

hints.1: Ask what runs automatically at construction and what self points at.
hints.2: Contrast self.name = name with a plain local name = name inside __init__.
hints.3: __init__ initializes instance attributes on creation; self is that instance; omitting self from def bark(): makes buddy.bark() raise TypeError because Python still passes the instance.

phases.goal: Decide when a class is warranted versus grouping functions another way.

must_hit.point: Do not use a class merely to group standalone functions that share no state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate rejects empty/stateless 'utility classes' used only as function bags.

must_hit.point: For standalone functions with no shared state, prefer a module instead of a class.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says use a module when there is no per-instance state to share.

probes: When would you put related functions in a class versus in a module?

hints.1: Ask whether those functions share any object state.
hints.2: If nothing is stored on instances, a class adds little beyond a namespace.
hints.3: No shared state → module; shared state plus behavior on instances → class.

phases.goal: Apply class design so multiple instances keep independent state and methods update that state.

must_hit.point: Independent instances keep separate state via self (e.g. alice_account and bob_account have separate balances).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains two BankAccount objects do not share balance because each uses its own self.

must_hit.point: Instance methods can modify that instance's state (e.g. deposit increases self.balance when amount > 0).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate shows or describes deposit updating only the receiver's balance.

must_hit.point: __init__ can take constructor parameters and defaults (e.g. owner and starting_balance) to set initial instance attributes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate wires __init__(self, owner, starting_balance=0) into self.owner and self.balance.

must_hit.point: Once objects hold state, the next concern is protecting that state from invalid values, which leads to encapsulation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate links stateful objects to the need for encapsulation next.

probes: Walk through a BankAccount (or similar) class: how do two accounts stay independent, and how does a method change one account's balance?

hints.1: Picture two accounts created from the same class with different owners.
hints.2: Trace self.balance on each instance through __init__ and deposit.
hints.3: alice_account = BankAccount("Alice", 100) and bob_account = BankAccount("Bob") keep separate balances; alice_account.deposit(50) updates only Alice's balance via self.

tradeoffs.topic: Class vs module for grouping functions
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use a class when you need per-instance state bundled with methods that operate on that state. If you only have standalone functions that share no state, put them in a module instead of a class.

gotchas.trap: Defining an instance method without self as the first parameter (e.g. def bark():).
gotchas.correction: Python still passes the instance as the first argument on buddy.bark(), so the call raises TypeError; write def bark(self):.

gotchas.trap: Assigning attributes in __init__ without self (treating them as ordinary locals).
gotchas.correction: Those names disappear when __init__ finishes; use self.name = name (and similar) so the data is attached to the instance permanently.

gotchas.trap: Using a class only as a bag of standalone functions with no shared state.
gotchas.correction: That is a poor fit for classes; use a module for that grouping instead.
